title: Introduction to Maps
text:
What Is GIS?
Geographic Information Systems = data + location

Any dataset with a spatial component can be put on a map
Agriculture is inherently spatial: counties, farms, markets, watersheds, supply chains
Maps reveal patterns that tables and charts simply cannot


Today’s goal: get you from zero to a working map pipeline in R

GIS has historically required specialized software (ArcGIS, QGIS). R has changed that dramatically. You can do most of what you’d do in ArcGIS from a .R script.

Almost all the data you’ll encounter in agricultural economics is vector data. County-level NASS stats map to polygons. Farmers market locations map to points. Raster data comes up in remote sensing and climate work but we won’t need it today.

title: Introduction to Maps
section: What Lives in an sf Object?
text:
What Lives in an sf Object?
An sf data frame is just a regular data frame with one extra column: geometry
Simple feature collection with 3,234 features
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
CRS: NAD83 (EPSG:4269)

   GEOID  NAME         STATEFP  ALAND        geometry
1  01001  Autauga      01       1539602840   MULTIPOLYGON(...)
2  01003  Baldwin      01       4117521611   MULTIPOLYGON(...)
3  01005  Barbour      01       2291820706   MULTIPOLYGON(...)

The geometry column is a list of all the coordinate pairs (longitude, latitude) that define each shape. For a polygon, it’s every vertex. For a point, it’s just one.

This is the key insight that makes R spatial data so ergonomic. You don’t need to learn a new data model. filter(), mutate(), left_join() all work exactly as you’d expect.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems
The earth is round. Maps are flat. Something has to give.
A CRS defines how 3D coordinates get projected onto a 2D surface.

Two CRS you’ll use constantly:








CRS
EPSG
When you’ll see it




WGS84
4326
GPS coordinates, GeoJSON files, web APIs, mapgl


Albers Equal Area
5070
Thematic maps in ggplot2





Rule of thumb: store and share data in 4326. Project to 5070 for any static map of the contiguous US.

The most common beginner mistake is mixing CRS. If your layers don’t line up, 9 times out of 10 it’s a mismatch. sf will warn you but always check. You reproject with st_transform(your_data, 5070).

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Getting Boundary Data

TIGER/Line files: the Census Bureau’s authoritative geographic boundary dataset, covering states, counties, tracts, roads, water features, and more
tigris: an R package that downloads TIGER/Line files directly from the Census API and returns them as sf objects, ready to map


states_sf <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m") %>%
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI", "PR", "VI", "GU", "AS", "MP"))

counties_sf <- counties(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m") %>%
  filter(!STATEFP %in% c("02", "15", "72", "78", "66", "60", "69"))


cb = TRUE: simplified cartographic boundary (better for maps)
resolution = "20m": 1:20,000,000 scale (right for national maps)
The filter removes Alaska, Hawaii, and territories


tigris has many other geographies too: tracts, block groups, places, school districts, congressional districts, ZIP codes, roads, water features. All come back as sf objects ready to use.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Real Data: LACE
New from the Census Bureau: county-level estimates of households without air conditioning.

lace <- read_csv("https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/datasets/lace/2023/LACE_23_County.csv") %>%
  mutate(GEOID = paste0(STATE, COUNTY))

lace_map <- counties_sf %>%
  left_join(lace, by = "GEOID")

This is the standard workflow: get boundaries from tigris, join your data on GEOID, map it.

GEOID is the 5-character FIPS code: 2-digit state + 3-digit county, always zero-padded. This is the universal join key for any Census-derived county data.

    labels = percent, name = "Share without A/C"

  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = .5)) +

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Color Scale Options

# Sequential (one hue, light to dark)
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGn", direction = 1)
scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket")

# Diverging (two hues, use when 0 means something)
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = 1)

# Right-skewed data: log-transform the scale
scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = scales::comma)


Avoid rainbow palettes (rainbow(), jet). They are not perceptually uniform and create false visual boundaries in your data.


ColorBrewer (colorbrewer2.org) — designed by cartographer Cynthia Brewer, it provides rigorously tested sequential, diverging, and qualitative palettes optimized for maps. No need to reinvent the wheel; the cartographers already laid the groundwork.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Pulling SNAP Data with Geometry

snap_households <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(snap  = "B22003_002",
                total = "B22003_001"),
  year      = 2022,
  geometry  = TRUE
) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) %>%
  mutate(snap_pct = snap / total) %>%
  filter(!str_starts(GEOID, "02|15|72"))

geometry = TRUE is the killer feature: one call returns data and boundaries together.

Going Smaller: Census Tracts

  geography = "tract", state = "RI",
  variables = c(snap = "B22003_002", total = "B22003_001"),

  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) %>%
  mutate(snap_pct = snap / total) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = snap_pct), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "A", direction = -1,
                       labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                       na.value = "grey90") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "SNAP Participation by Census Tract, Rhode Island",
       subtitle = "2020-2024 5-year ACS Estimates")

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Finding Better Breaks: Jenks
Right-skewed ag data looks like one color with a linear scale. Jenks natural breaks fix that.

corn_vals <- as.numeric(str_remove_all(corn_acres_sf$corn_acres_planted, ","))
soy_vals  <- as.numeric(str_remove_all(soybean_acres_sf$soybean_acres_planted, ","))
combined  <- c(corn_vals, soy_vals)

brks <- classIntervals(
  combined[!is.na(combined) & combined > 0], n = 5, style = "jenks"
)$brks %>% round(-3)

pal <- brewer.pal(length(brks), "YlGn")

Using the combined distribution ensures both maps share the same color scale.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Comparing Maps with compare()

left_map <- maplibre(bounds = states_sf, style = carto_style("voyager")) %>%
  add_fill_layer(id = "corn_acres", source = corn_acres_sf,
    fill_color = interpolate(column = "corn_acres_planted",
                             values = brks, stops = pal, na_color = "lightgrey"),
    fill_opacity = 0.9, tooltip = "corn_acres_planted") %>%
  add_line_layer(id = "states", source = states_sf, line_width = .1) %>%
  add_continuous_legend("Corn Acres Planted, 2015",
    values = brks, colors = pal, position = "top-left")

right_map <- maplibre(bounds = states_sf, style = carto_style("voyager")) %>%
  add_fill_layer(id = "soybean_acres", source = soybean_acres_sf,
    fill_color = interpolate(column = "soybean_acres_planted",
                             values = brks, stops = pal, na_color = "lightgrey"),
    fill_opacity = 0.9, tooltip = "soybean_acres_planted") %>%
  add_line_layer(id = "states", source = states_sf, line_width = .1) %>%
  add_continuous_legend("Soybean Acres Planted, 2015",
    values = brks, colors = pal, position = "top-left")

compare(left_map, right_map, height = "900px")

st_as_sf(): Adding Geometry

usda_inspection_estabs_sf <- usda_inspection_estabs %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~iconv(., to = "UTF-8", sub = ""))) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 5070)

lower48_usda <- st_intersection(
  usda_inspection_estabs_sf,
  st_transform(states_sf, 5070)
) %>%
  filter(size %in% c("Large", "Small", "Very Small"))

st_as_sf() turns lat/lon columns into a geometry column. After that, it’s a normal sf object.

  st_as_sf(wkt = "geometry_wkt", crs = 4326) %>%

county_pop_2020 <- get_decennial(geography = "county", variables = "P1_001N",
  year = 2020, geometry = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(5070) %>%
  filter(!str_starts(GEOID, "02|15|72")) %>%
  select(cty_fips = GEOID, pop20 = value)

dollar_store_sf <- st_intersection(dollar_stores, county_pop_2020) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(dollar_stores = n(), pop_2020 = first(pop20), .by = cty_fips) %>%
  replace_na(list(dollar_stores = 0)) %>%
  mutate(dollar_stores_per_capita = dollar_stores / pop_2020) %>%
  right_join(county_pop_2020, by = "cty_fips") %>%
  st_as_sf()

title: Putting Farm Credit Branches on the Map
text:
Photo by Taylor Siebert on Unsplash.
The Farm Credit System (FCS) is a nationwide network of borrower-owned lending cooperatives created by Congress in 1916 to ensure that farmers, ranchers, and rural residents have reliable access to credit.1 Today the FCS operates through roughly 60 regional lenders, each serving a defined geographic territory.2 As of 2021, the system held 45 percent of all U.S. farm sector debt, more than any other lender category in the country.3 The whole network is regulated and examined by the Farm Credit Administration (FCA), a federal agency established “to ensure that Farm Credit System institutions…are safe, sound, and dependable sources of credit.”4
Fair warning before diving in: I am a regional economist and not an ag finance scholar! My interest in Farm Credit grows out of some ongoing work on “bank deserts” and the downstream economic consequences that follow. In that research, we have tried to incorporate credit unions and Farm Credit associations alongside FDIC-regulated branches. The problem is that unlike FDIC and NCUA data, which are freely available and well-structured, the geographic locations of Farm Credit branches and headquarters are surprisingly difficult to pin down.
Back in 2022, I cobbled together a time-consuming method to collect Farm Credit branch addresses, state by state. That approach worked out okay, but it isn’t something I would care to repeat. As we continue building out our research on brick-and-mortar lending access,5 I wanted a cleaner, more reproducible pipeline. And with the assistance of Claude Code, I built one!
I shared an early draft of this post with Jennifer Ifft, Kevin Kim, Joe Parcell, and Alice Roach—agricultural economists who each know far more about the Farm Credit System than I do—and their feedback sharpened the text and directly informed the What’s Next section below. I am grateful for their time and generosity.

title: Putting Farm Credit Branches on the Map
text:
Mapping the Farm Credit System
Branch office locations were scraped from the Farm Credit “Find a Lender” tool, which enables a county-level lender search. To get complete national coverage, I queried every county in every state and deduplicated the results. Headquarters addresses came from a separate source: the FCA Public Directory, which lists every chartered institution along with its official address. I scraped the detail page for each institution, parsed the address into its component fields, and fuzzy-joined the results to the Farm Credit organization names to produce a unified dataset of branch and headquarters locations across the country.

title: Putting Farm Credit Branches on the Map
text:
What’s Next
Several directions worth exploring came out of the reviewer feedback.
County service territories. Each Farm Credit lender has an officially designated set of counties where it is authorized to originate loans. The FCA Public Directory lists these territories for every institution, and mapping them would reveal something the branch-location map cannot: where multiple ACAs hold overlapping authority and compete for the same borrowers, versus where a single lender operates without competition. There is an important nuance here, though. As Joe noted, county lines are becoming a less reliable proxy for actual service area; if a borrower initiates contact, a lender can legally service that customer anywhere in the US.
Institutional complexity. The current map treats all branches as interchangeable, but the underlying institutional landscape is more varied than it appears. Making that structure legible on a map is a genuine challenge: with roughly 55 associations, color alone cannot do the work, and even a well-designed association-level visualization would require careful handling of entities that appear independent on paper but operate as one. Farm Credit Services of America, Frontier Farm Credit, and AgCountry share a single board and leadership team; their Manhattan, KS and Fargo, ND offices function as branches in practice, even though the FCA classifies them as headquarters. A different, less consolidated arrangement exists under AgVantis, which pools back-office services across six associations without yet merging governance.
Branch granularity and map density. Jenny pointed out that not all “branches” are equivalent: in Kansas, some locations are outposts, open only a few days a week, which creates a different access picture than a full-service branch. It may be possible to recover this distinction from the FCA web tool. She also noted that the size of the plotted points gives an impression of a denser network than actually exists; overlaying county boundaries would help ground the map in the vast rural territories each office is meant to serve.

Code for ggplot2 map
This code aggregates business locations into H3 hexagons at resolution 3 (approximately 4,800 square miles each), counts the number of establishments per hexagon, and clips the results to the contiguous United States. The ggplot2 visualization uses an Albers Equal Area projection and a yellow-green color scale to show the spatial distribution of businesses with “Kountry” in their name.
I use data from the YourEconomy Time Series (YTS), which covers all U.S. business establishments from 1998 to 2025. For legal reasons—i.e., it’s their data, not mine—that data is not provided in this repository.

library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(sf)
library(h3jsr)
library(tigris)
library(mapgl)

# Contiguous 48 states
states <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = '20m') |>
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI") & STATEFP < 60)

ytsdb <- open_dataset('data/yts')
df <- ytsdb |>
  filter(year %in% c(2021:2025), str_detect(tolower(company), 'kountry')) |>
  collect() |>
  filter(state != 'HI' & state != 'AK')

# Clean and prepare spatial data
dsf <- df |>
  mutate(longitude = ifelse(longitude > 0, longitude * -1, longitude)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) |>
  st_transform(6350) |> # Transform to Albers
  slice(1, .by = id)

# H3 requires WGS84, so transform back temporarily
dsf <- dsf |>
  mutate(h3_index = point_to_cell(st_transform(geometry, 4326), res = 3))

# Count occurrences per hexagon
hex_counts <- dsf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(h3_index, name = "count")

# Convert H3 indices to polygons
hex_sf <- hex_counts |>
  mutate(geometry = cell_to_polygon(h3_index)) |>
  st_as_sf(crs = 4326)

states <- states |> st_transform(6350) |> select(st = STUSPS)
hex_sf <- hex_sf |> st_transform(6350) |> st_intersection(states)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = '#FFFFE5', color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = hex_sf, aes(fill = count), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = .15) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = 'YlGn',
    direction = 1,
    name = 'Count',
    limits = c(0, 12)
  ) +
  theme_void(base_family = 'Red Hat Display', base_size = 14) +
  labs(
    title = "Density of Business Establishments with 'Kountry' in the Name",
    subtitle = '(Each Hexagon ≈ 4,800 square miles)',
    caption = '\nSource: YourEconomy Time Series, 2025    \n'
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "italic", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = 'bottom'
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_colourbar(
      barheight = 0.5,
      barwidth = 12,
      title.position = "top"
    )
  )

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
A household is conventionally called rent burdened when gross rent takes up 30 percent or more of household income.1 By that definition, roughly half of American renters are burdened, and the share has been climbing since 2019. This post takes ACS table B25070 at two non-overlapping five-year windows—2015-2019 and 2020-2024—and maps where the increase landed.
One bit of housekeeping before anything else. Writing out both endpoints every time gets unbearable, so from here on a single year is shorthand for the five-year window ending in it: 2019 means the 2015-2019 estimates, 2024 means 2020-2024. That is the Census Bureau’s own labeling and it is how you ask for the files (get_acs(year = 2024) returns 2020-2024). Where the window itself is the point, as in the next section, the full range is spelled out.
The short version: the national share went from 49.6 percent to 51.1 percent, the increase is concentrated in metropolitan counties rather than rural ones, and it is heavily a Sun Belt story. Nevada, Florida, Texas, Arizona and Georgia lead, and in Nevada every single county got worse.
Everything below runs from this one file. The complete script is at the bottom of the post.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
The long view
Picking two years a decade apart would have been the obvious move, but it would have been a mistake. Rent burden is not on a trend, it is on a U-shaped curve. Here’s every ACS five-year estimate ever published, from 2005-2009 through to 2020-2024:









The peak sits at 2009-2013 and 2010-2014, right after the foreclosure crisis pushed a wave of former owners into the rental market. The “trough” is 2016-2020. Since then it has risen every single year.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
Pulling the data
B25070 breaks renter households into bins by the share of income they spend on gross rent. Anything from _007 up is 30 percent or more. Line _001 is the total, but it includes _011, the households whose ratio could not be computed (zero or negative income, no cash rent), so that group comes out of the denominator.
Margins of error are carried through the whole calculation, because they turn out to be an important part of the story. Weighting by renter households, the national burdened share went from 49.6% to 51.1%, and the median county moved +0.6 points.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
section: Where it is worst right now
text:
Where it is worst right now
Everything after this section is about change. Before getting there it is worth looking at the level, because the two are not the same map.






Florida is the most rent-burdened state in the country: 60.1% of its renters hand over at least 30 percent of their income, against 51.1 percent nationally. Broward, Miami-Dade and Palm Beach counties all clear 62 percent. Hawaii, Nevada and California come next.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
The raw change






The map above is mostly wrong. Those familiar with the ACS will immediately know why.
The ACS is a sample, and in a county with only a few hundred renter households, the margin of error on a five-year change runs past ±18 points. Only 21% of counties have a change a 90 percent confidence interval can tell apart from zero.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
Shrinking out the noise
Rather than blanking those counties out, let’s shrink them. Comparing the spread of the estimates against their own margins of error yields an estimate of how much the true county changes actually vary; each county’s estimate is then blended with a prior in proportion to its own precision. A well-measured county keeps its own number, a hopeless one leans almost entirely on the prior, and those in between land somewhere in the middle. Importantly, every county still appears on the map.2
One obvious-seeming choice to remedy this problem is to rely on the county’s state average. However, because this strategy pulls smaller counties’ estimates toward the statewide average, it really just ends up making the state look just like its largest metro (Clark County holds 77 percent of Nevada’s weight, and Maricopa 64 percent of Arizona’s, to give two examples). This can also yield hard discontinuities at state lines, leading keen observers to be immediately distrustful of what they’re looking at.
To get around that issue, we use each county’s neighbors instead, a widely used strategy in disease mapping.3 Going back to our Nevada example, Nye County would borrow from Clark because Pahrump is a true Las Vegas exurb, while Eureka County, three hundred miles to the north, would not.
The between-county standard deviation of the true change comes out to 5.0 points, against an observed spread of 10.4. Roughly 77% of the variation in the first map is sampling noise. Note the narrower scale below.






For the median county, the posterior mean (we’ll call it the shrinkage estimate from here on) draws 40% of its weight from the county’s own data, rising to 87% among the largest counties.

The 82 counties with more than 100,000 renter households hold 48 percent of the country’s renters between them, and 83 percent of them got worse. Rural America is roughly where it was in 2019, while the places where most people actually rent are not.
This is about what supply and demand would predict. Demand has been arriving in Las Vegas, the Dallas suburbs and Central Florida, and rents went with it. The places people have been moving to are the places where rent gets bid up. The rural end is where intuition tends to mislead us. Just because rural places are typically associated with higher poverty rates and lower incomes doesn’t mean the housing affordability crisis of recent years would automatically hit them the hardest. Rents there are lower to begin with, and they have not been bid up the same way.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
Moving the Threshold
A fair objection to all of this is that 30 percent is an arbitrary line. A household at 29 percent and one at 31 percent are not meaningfully different, and if the increase were really just households drifting across that boundary, then tightening the definition should make most of it disappear.
So what happens if we move the threshold for what it means to be “rent-burdened”? The two maps below repeat the shrinkage estimates at stricter cuts, first for renters paying 40 percent or more of their income and then for those paying 50 percent or more. Same window, same neighbor shrinkage, and the same color scale as before, so all three can be read against each other directly.

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
Concluding Thoughts
While I do have a few papers that focus on housing, I wouldn’t really consider myself a housing researcher. Truly, I only decided to make this map because I was fiddling around with data.census.gov while writing a problem set for my data science class…I saw the rent burden variable and thought, ‘Hmmm, that might make for an interesting map!’
And yet, even for someone without housing policy chops such as myself, there are a few things here that are worth pointing out.
The answer depends almost entirely on which year you start from. Run this same analysis from 2014 and you get -1.2 points, and you would write a post about rent burden easing. Run it from 2019 and you get +1.5 points. Neither number is wrong. The first one just happens to start at the worst moment in modern rental affordability and is therefore measuring a recovery from the foreclosure crisis, not anything about the last five years. This is the sort of thing that makes me nervous about any chart with two endpoints and nothing in between.
Where people moved is where rent got worse. The increases are not spread evenly, and they are not in the places that get written about as expensive. They are in Las Vegas, in the Atlanta and Dallas suburbs, in Nashville, and across most of Florida. These are the destinations of the past five years, and the rental stock does not appear to have kept up.
This is now a metropolitan problem. The largest fifth of counties, holding 86 percent of American renters, rose +1.7 points. Rural counties went essentially nowhere. Whatever national average you quote is really a statement about big metros.
It is not an artifact of the 30 percent line. If households were merely drifting from just under the threshold to just over it, the stricter cuts would barely move. They move nearly as much: the 40 percent share is up 1.3 points and the 50 percent share up 1.2. More renters are severely burdened than five years ago, which is the number I think matters.
So the rhetoric about rent being unaffordable is not wrong. It just does not describe the whole country evenly, and it describes the last five years far better than it describes the last ten.
Source. ACS 5-year estimates, table B25070, via tidycensus. Geometry from tigris at 20m generalized resolution.

      end = y,
      renters = v001E - v011E,
      `30% or more` = 100 * (v007E + v008E + v009E + v010E) / renters,
      `50% or more` = 100 * v010E / renters
    )
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  pivot_longer(c(`30% or more`, `50% or more`),
               names_to = "threshold", values_to = "pct")

ends <- filter(series, end %in% c(2019, 2024))

# Each threshold gets its own y scale. On a shared axis the 3-point swing in a
# 50-point range reads as a flat line, which is exactly what the chart is
# meant to argue against.
ggplot(series, aes(end, pct, color = threshold)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2018.6, xmax = 2019.4, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.3) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2023.6, xmax = 2024.4, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = ends, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct)),
            vjust = -1.2, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~threshold, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("30% or more" = "#b2182b", "50% or more" = "#2166ac")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2009, 2024, 3),
                     labels = \(x) paste0(x - 4, "-\n", x)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.2))) +
  labs(
    title = "Rent burden peaked after the foreclosure crisis, fell, then turned around",
    subtitle = "Share of renter households spending 30% or more, and 50% or more, of income on gross rent",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates, table B25070. Each panel has its own vertical scale.\nShaded bands mark the two windows mapped below."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.y = unit(14, "pt"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey50", hjust = 0),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )

# ---- pull-acs ------------------------------------------------------
# Standard Census formulas for derived estimates: root-sum-square for sums and differences, and the proportion formula for a share. Written out so they stay vectorized over the whole data frame.
moe_rss <- function(...) sqrt(rowSums(cbind(...)^2))
moe_share <- function(num, den, m_num, m_den) {
  p <- num / den
  under <- m_num^2 - (p^2 * m_den^2)
  # Negative radicand: fall back to the ratio formula, per Census guidance
  sqrt(ifelse(under < 0, m_num^2 + (p^2 * m_den^2), under)) / den
}

pull_burden <- function(year, geometry = FALSE) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county", variables = VARS, year = year, survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide", geometry = geometry,
    resolution = "20m",   # generalized boundaries: ~50x smaller, plots faster
    cache_table = TRUE
  ) |>
    rename_with(\(x) str_replace(x, "^B25070_", "v"), starts_with("B25070_")) |>
    mutate(
      renters      = v001E - v011E,
      renters      = if_else(renters > 0, renters, NA_real_),
      renters_moe  = moe_rss(v001M, v011M),
      burdened     = v007E + v008E + v009E + v010E,
      burdened_moe = moe_rss(v007M, v008M, v009M, v010M),
      pct          = 100 * burdened / renters,
      pct_moe      = 100 * moe_share(burdened, renters, burdened_moe, renters_moe),
      # The same measure at stricter thresholds: 40%+ is bins _009 and _010, 50%+ is _010 on its own.
      pct40        = 100 * (v009E + v010E) / renters,
      pct40_moe    = 100 * moe_share(v009E + v010E, renters, moe_rss(v009M, v010M), renters_moe),
      pct50        = 100 * v010E / renters,
      pct50_moe    = 100 * moe_share(v010E, renters, v010M, renters_moe)
    ) |>
    select(GEOID, NAME, any_of("geometry"), renters, burdened,
           pct, pct_moe, pct40, pct40_moe, pct50, pct50_moe)
}

b19 <- pull_burden(2019)
b24 <- pull_burden(2024, geometry = TRUE)

# ---- build-change --------------------------------------------------
burden <- b24 |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, renters_24 = renters, burdened_24 = burdened,
         pct_24 = pct, pct_24_moe = pct_moe,
         pct40_24 = pct40, pct40_24_moe = pct40_moe,
         pct50_24 = pct50, pct50_24_moe = pct50_moe) |>
  separate_wider_delim(NAME, ", ", names = c("county", "state"),
                       too_many = "merge") |>
  inner_join(
    b19 |> select(GEOID, renters_19 = renters, burdened_19 = burdened,
                  pct_19 = pct, pct_19_moe = pct_moe,
                  pct40_19 = pct40, pct40_19_moe = pct40_moe,
                  pct50_19 = pct50, pct50_19_moe = pct50_moe),
    by = "GEOID"
  ) |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  mutate(
    change       = pct_24 - pct_19,
    change_moe   = moe_rss(pct_24_moe, pct_19_moe),
    sig          = abs(change) > change_moe,   # 90% CI excludes zero
    change40     = pct40_24 - pct40_19,
    change40_moe = moe_rss(pct40_24_moe, pct40_19_moe),
    change50     = pct50_24 - pct50_19,
    change50_moe = moe_rss(pct50_24_moe, pct50_19_moe)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(change)) |>
  st_transform(4326)   # mapgl wants lon/lat; the ggplot maps get shifted later

# The interactive maps each embed their own copy of the boundaries, so they get a simplified one. ms_simplify works on the shared topology rather than polygon by polygon, so counties still tile with no slivers between them. keep = 0.35 takes about a third off the payload while leaving coastlines like the Mississippi delta still recognisable when a reader zooms in; much lower than that and they visibly polygonise.
geom_ll <- burden |>
  select(GEOID) |>
  rmapshaper::ms_simplify(keep = 0.35, keep_shapes = TRUE)

# State outlines dissolved from the same simplified boundaries, so the overlay lines up with the county edges exactly.
states_ll <- geom_ll |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(burden) |> select(GEOID, state), by = "GEOID") |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop")

us48 <- states_ll |> filter(!state %in% c("Alaska", "Hawaii", "Puerto Rico"))

# Attaches just the columns a given map needs to the light geometry.
map_sf <- function(...) {
  geom_ll |>
    left_join(st_drop_geometry(burden) |> transmute(GEOID, ...), by = "GEOID") |>
    select(-GEOID)
}

# Diverging ramp matching the static maps further down.
div_pal <- colorRampPalette(c("#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"))

# ---- map-level -----------------------------------------------------
lvl <- burden |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(level = weighted.mean(pct_24, renters_24),
            chg   = weighted.mean(change, renters_24), .groups = "drop")

lvl_sf <- map_sf(
    pct_24,
    tooltip = glue(
      "<b>{county}, {state}</b><br>",
      "{sprintf('%.1f', pct_24)}% of renters pay 30%+ of income<br>",
      "{comma(round(renters_24))} renter households"
    )
)

maplibre(bounds = us48, style = carto_style("positron")) |>
  add_source(id = "counties", data = lvl_sf) |>
  add_fill_layer(
    id = "Rent burden",
    source = "counties",
    fill_color = interpolate(
      column = "pct_24", values = c(35, 50, 65),
      stops = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "YlOrRd"), na_color = "lightgrey"
    ),
    fill_opacity = 0.85,
    tooltip = "tooltip"
  ) |>
  add_line_layer(id = "county_outlines", source = "counties",
                 line_color = "black", line_width = 0.05) |>
  add_line_layer(id = "state_outlines", source = states_ll,
                 line_color = "black", line_width = 0.4) |>
  add_continuous_legend(
    "Renters paying 30%+ of income, 2024",
    values = c("35%", "50%", "65%+"),
    colors = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "YlOrRd"),
    position = "bottom-left"
  )

# ---- map-helper ----------------------------------------------------
# Both static maps are the same diverging choropleth, differing only in the column they fill by and how wide the scale runs.
burden_map <- function(col, cap, title, subtitle, thresh = 30) {
  ggplot(burden_sh) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[col]]), color = NA) +
    geom_sf(data = states_sh, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#2166ac", mid = "#f7f7f7", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-cap, cap), oob = scales::squish,
      labels = \(x) sprintf("%+g", x),
      name = sprintf("Change in share of\nrenters paying %d%%+\nof income (pp)", thresh),
      guide = guide_colorbar(barheight = 10, barwidth = 0.8)
    ) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle,
         caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates, table B25070. AK, HI and PR shifted and rescaled; CT omitted (2022 planning-region change).") +
    theme_void(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 8)),
      plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey50", hjust = 0),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9, lineheight = 1.1),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
    )
}

# ---- map-raw -------------------------------------------------------
raw_sf <- map_sf(
    change,
    tooltip = glue(
      "<b>{county}, {state}</b><br>",
      "Change since 2019: {sprintf('%+.1f', change)} pp<br>",
      "Margin of error: ±{sprintf('%.1f', change_moe)} pp<br>",
      "{comma(round(renters_24))} renter households"
    )
)

maplibre(bounds = us48, style = carto_style("positron")) |>
  add_source(id = "counties", data = raw_sf) |>
  add_fill_layer(
    id = "Raw change",
    source = "counties",
    fill_color = interpolate(
      column = "change", values = c(-15, 0, 15),
      stops = div_pal(3), na_color = "lightgrey"
    ),
    fill_opacity = 0.85,
    tooltip = "tooltip"
  ) |>
  add_line_layer(id = "county_outlines", source = "counties",
                 line_color = "black", line_width = 0.05) |>
  add_line_layer(id = "state_outlines", source = states_ll,
                 line_color = "black", line_width = 0.4) |>
  add_continuous_legend(
    "Change in share paying 30%+ of income (pp)",
    values = c("-15", "0", "+15"),
    colors = div_pal(3),
    position = "bottom-left"
  )

# ---- shrinkage -----------------------------------------------------
# Queen contiguity. The seven island counties (Nantucket, Kauai, Vieques and friends) have no land neighbors, so they borrow from their five nearest by centroid instead.
nb  <- poly2nb(burden, queen = TRUE, snap = 1000)
knn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(st_centroid(st_geometry(burden)), k = 5))
for (i in which(card(nb) == 0)) nb[[i]] <- knn[[i]]

# Observed change y = truth + sampling error, with SE = MOE/1.645 (ACS margins are 90%). The prior for each county is the precision-weighted mean of its neighbors' changes, so a well-measured neighbor counts for more than a noisy one. Between-county variance tau^2 comes from Paule-Mandel: the value that makes the chi-square residual around the prior come out at its expectation, so no cutoff is chosen by hand. Written as a function because the stricter thresholds further down get the same treatment.
shrink <- function(y, moe) {
  se    <- moe / 1.645
  w     <- 1 / pmax(se, 1e-6)^2
  prior <- map_dbl(nb, \(nn) sum(w[nn] * y[nn]) / sum(w[nn]))
  s2    <- se^2
  gap   <- function(t2) sum((y - prior)^2 / (s2 + t2)) - (length(y) - 1)
  tau2  <- if (gap(0) <= 0) 0 else uniroot(gap, c(0, 1e4))$root
  B     <- s2 / (s2 + tau2)
  list(eb = (1 - B) * y + B * prior, B = B, tau2 = tau2, prior = prior)
}

fit  <- shrink(burden$change, burden$change_moe)
tau2 <- fit$tau2

burden <- burden |>
  mutate(
    nbr_prior   = fit$prior,
    B           = fit$B,
    change_eb   = fit$eb,
    reliability = 1 - fit$B,   # 0 = all borrowed, 1 = all own data
    change40_eb = shrink(change40, change40_moe)$eb,
    change50_eb = shrink(change50, change50_moe)$eb
  )

# The threshold maps and the listing thumbnail stay static, so they get their own copy with AK, HI and PR shifted into insets. Built here, once every shrunk column exists.
burden_sh <- shift_geometry(burden)
states_sh <- burden_sh |> group_by(state) |> summarise(.groups = "drop")

# ---- map-eb --------------------------------------------------------
eb_sf <- map_sf(
    change_eb,
    tooltip = glue(
      "<b>{county}, {state}</b><br>",
      "Shrinkage estimate: {sprintf('%+.1f', change_eb)} pp<br>",
      "Raw estimate: {sprintf('%+.1f', change)} ± {sprintf('%.1f', change_moe)} pp<br>",
      "Weight on its own data: {sprintf('%.0f', 100*reliability)}%"
    )
)

maplibre(bounds = us48, style = carto_style("positron")) |>
  add_source(id = "counties", data = eb_sf) |>
  add_fill_layer(
    id = "Shrinkage estimate",
    source = "counties",
    fill_color = interpolate(
      column = "change_eb", values = c(-8, 0, 8),
      stops = div_pal(3), na_color = "lightgrey"
    ),
    fill_opacity = 0.85,
    tooltip = "tooltip"
  ) |>
  add_line_layer(id = "county_outlines", source = "counties",
                 line_color = "black", line_width = 0.05) |>
  add_line_layer(id = "state_outlines", source = states_ll,
                 line_color = "black", line_width = 0.4) |>
  add_continuous_legend(
    "Change in share paying 30%+ of income (pp)",
    values = c("-8", "0", "+8"),
    colors = div_pal(3),
    position = "bottom-left"
  )

# ---- thumbnail -----------------------------------------------------
# Bare version of the map above, written to disk for the blog listing thumbnail. No title, legend, caption or margins. Sized 4:3 to match the listing's crop so nothing gets cut off.
ggsave(
  "thumbnail.png",
  burden_map("change_eb", 8, NULL, NULL) +
    labs(caption = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "none", plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0)),
  width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150
)

# ---- where ---------------------------------------------------------
bd <- st_drop_geometry(burden)

top_states <- bd |>
  group_by(State = state) |>
  summarise(
    Counties = n(),
    `Renters (000s)` = round(sum(renters_24) / 1e3),
    m30 = weighted.mean(change_eb, renters_24),
    m50 = weighted.mean(change50_eb, renters_24),
    `Counties rising` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(change_eb > 0)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(m30)) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(`30%+` = sprintf("%+.1f", m30), `50%+` = sprintf("%+.1f", m50), .keep = "unused") |>
  relocate(`Counties rising`, .after = last_col())

# Counties big enough that the estimate is mostly their own data
big <- bd |>
  filter(renters_24 > 100000) |>
  summarise(n = n(), renters = sum(renters_24),
            chg = weighted.mean(pct_24, renters_24) - weighted.mean(pct_19, renters_19),
            red = 100 * mean(change_eb > 0))

cat(knitr::kable(top_states, align = "lrrrrr",
                 caption = "States by renter-weighted change in the 30%+ share, 2019 to 2024."),
    sep = "\n")

# ---- map-40 --------------------------------------------------------
burden_map("change40_eb", 8,
  "Renters paying 40% or more of their income toward rent",
  "",
  thresh = 40)

# ---- map-50 --------------------------------------------------------
burden_map("change50_eb", 8,
  "Renters paying 50% or more of their income toward rent",
  "",
  thresh = 50)

# ---- download ------------------------------------------------------
# Encode the tidied table straight into the page as a data URI, so the post stays a single file with no data sidecars in the repo.
csv <- burden |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(GEOID, county, state, renters_19, renters_24,
         pct_19, pct_24, change, change_moe, change_eb, reliability, sig) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  format_csv()

cat(sprintf(
  '<a href="data:text/csv;base64,%s" download="rent_burden.csv" class="btn btn-primary">Download CSV</a>',
  jsonlite::base64_enc(charToRaw(csv))
))

title: Rent Burden Is Climbing Again
text:
Footnotes


The 30 percent threshold was codified by the Brooke Amendment, which capped public housing rents at 25 percent of income in 1969; Congress raised the figure to 30 percent in 1981. It is the definition behind HUD’s cost-burden programs, the Census Bureau’s own published cost-burden tables, and the annual State of the Nation’s Housing reports from Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. It is worth knowing that the number is a policy artifact rather than an empirical finding: it descends from an old rule of thumb that a week’s wages should cover a month’s rent.↩︎
Almost every county, anyway. Joining the two vintages on GEOID quietly drops those whose codes changed in between. Connecticut replaced its eight counties with nine planning regions in 2022 and so has no overlap at all, which is why the state is blank on every map here. Alaska also split Valdez-Cordova into Chugach and Copper River. That is nine counties lost on the 2019 side and eleven on the 2024 side. Puerto Rico’s 78 municipios are included throughout.↩︎
Besag, J., York, J., & Mollié, A. (1991). Bayesian image restoration, with two applications in spatial statistics. Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics, 43(1), 1-20. The same idea underpins the Census Bureau’s own small-area programs, SAIPE and SAHIE, which use the closely related Fay-Herriot model.↩︎

title: The 2025 County Population Data Is Out. Here’s What It Shows.
text: Today marks the release of the latest batch of data from the U.S. Census Bureau: the 2025 County Population Totals and Components of Change. Below is a collection of a few interactive maps that visualize changes that have taken place since last year, as well as a quick guide (including code snippets) for how to load, clean, and map the data.

title: The 2025 County Population Data Is Out. Here’s What It Shows.
text:
Components of Growth and Decline
Not all population growth looks the same. A county can be growing because it has more births than deaths, because people are moving in, or—ideally—both. Conversely, decline can stem from negative natural change (more deaths than births), outmigration, or both at once. The map below classifies every U.S. county into one of four categories based on its 2024–25 natural change and net migration:

What it means




Growing Both Ways

Births exceed deaths and people are moving in

Birth-Dependent

Declining Both Ways

Fewer births than deaths and net outmigration—the double squeeze









Perhaps the most striking takeaway from this map is just how spatially mixed the picture is. Even in states with strong overall population growth—Texas, Florida, the Carolinas—you’ll find pockets of birth-dependent or declining counties alongside booming ones. And in states often written off as uniformly shrinking, migration is quietly propping up growth in college towns, retirement destinations, and rural amenity counties. In general, county data catches nuance that state-level summaries often miss.
